name: Olga Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Olga. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any AI company, employer, union or party, and what you tell me stays confidential. Your name won't go on anything. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I get to Linden Road Health Centre about eight, with a coffee from the bakery under our flat, and I've got fifteen-minute appointments from half eight until twelve. It's coughs, blood pressure, a lot of anxiety and low mood, the odd rash nobody can name. Then lunch with Priya, one of our practice nurses, if we're lucky, and an afternoon of the same plus about forty test results and letters to sign off.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the regulars. There's a man with diabetes I've seen every three months since I started, and he now brings me his sugar readings in a little notebook, all neat. What wears me out is the admin after six: referral letters, forms for insurers, fitness-to-work notes. Most nights I'm still typing at seven while Tomas texts me asking if he should start dinner.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And money-wise, how do things sit at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fine, not flush. I'm salaried, seven sessions a week, a session being a half-day clinic, and Tomas is an electrician, so between us it's steady. We rent a two-bed above the bakery and we've got about four months of costs put away, which is meant to grow into a deposit for a flat. That's the plan, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start. The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds a lot like where we are now. The AI note-taker a couple of the partners use saves them maybe ten minutes a day, and that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I say now: it's a useful tool, not a doctor. In the staff room I'd probably joke that we were promised robots and got a slightly better spellchecker. I don't post about work online, so I'd leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it'd be a bit of a relief, because my job stays my job. But the things that actually hurt don't get fixed either: the waiting list, and the fact that we're two doctors short. I was half hoping AI would take the seven o'clock referral letters off me, and if it's mostly hype, I'll still be typing them at forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much carry on. I'd start using the note-taker properly instead of now and then, since it's been tested at our place for a year and nobody's had a problem. And Tomas and I would keep putting about four hundred a month aside so we can buy a flat in two or three years, probably out past the ring road where it's cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the job, tired about everything else. It's the normal kind of worry, the rent going up every January and whether I can keep doing fifty-hour weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the rent going up every January. What happens if it jumps again next year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the deposit takes longer, that's all. Last January it went up eighty a month and we just stopped eating out on Fridays. I'm not going to go hungry on a GP's salary, and I know how lucky that is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the practice would you worry about in this picture, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Dennis on reception, who's been on the front desk for twenty years. If the booking system gets even a bit smarter, the practice manager will want one fewer person there. Dennis knows every patient's grandmother, and no software is going to know that.

say: I'd call AI a **useful tool**, not a doctor, and joke that we got a better spellchecker.
I'd keep it in the staff room, because I **don't post about work** online.
think: My **job stays my job**, which is honestly a relief.
The real problems, the **waiting list** and the late-night letters, don't get fixed either.
do: **Use the note-taker** every day, now that it has been tested at the practice for a year.
Keep saving about **400 a month** with Tomas towards a flat past the ring road.
feel: **Calm** about the job, but **tired** of the long hours and rising rent.
S0.quote: I was half hoping AI would take the seven o'clock referral letters off me, and if it's mostly hype, I'll still be typing them at forty.
fieldNote: Her **disappointment** is that AI won't lift the paperwork, not that it threatens her.
She is **steady with tech**: she adopts the note-taker only after a year of colleagues using it.
Her first **worry is for others**, like the long-serving receptionist, not for herself.

steps.text: Keep working seven sessions a week at Linden Road Health Centre
Use the practice's AI note-taker in every clinic from January
Put 400 a month towards a flat deposit with Tomas

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one feels more real. A lot of what I do between patients is exactly that list: writing, checking, booking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good if it gets the letters and results off our desks, as long as a doctor still signs off. At the practice meeting I'd ask who checks the AI when it gets a result wrong. I'd be the sensible one, not the cheerleader and not the doom-monger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it changes how many of us they need. If AI drafts the letters and sorts the results, the partners will work out that six doctors can see what eight do now. I'm salaried, not a partner, so I'm the kind of doctor whose sessions get trimmed first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd go on whatever training the health board runs on the results software, once a few people I trust say it's worth it. I'd want to be the person who knows how it works, not the one it happens to. And I'd do the diploma in minor surgery and joint injections at the teaching hospital, because that's the part a computer can't do from a screen. It costs about 1,500, and I'd take it from the deposit savings if I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, maybe more than I'd admit at the meeting. Losing even one session a week would be real money, and it feels like the floor's tilting slightly and I need to keep my balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd pay for the course from the deposit fund. How does Tomas feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd grumble and then agree. Tomas always says a trade in your hands is worth more than a degree on the wall, so a course in stitching and injecting would win him over. We'd push the flat back maybe six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you won't go hungry on a GP's salary. Does that still hold here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly, yes. Even if I drop from seven sessions to six, that's still a decent wage, and there are two other practices within twenty minutes that are always short. I'm worried, but not frightened, and I think that's the honest place to be.

say: AI taking **letters and results** off our desks is good, as long as a doctor signs off.
I'd ask at the practice meeting **who checks the AI** when it gets a result wrong.
think: If AI drafts letters, **six doctors** could do the work of eight.
As a **salaried doctor**, not a partner, my sessions would be trimmed first.
do: Join the **health board training** on the results software once trusted colleagues vouch for it.
Take a **minor surgery diploma** at the teaching hospital for about **1,500**.
Push the **flat purchase** back about six months to pay for the course.
feel: **Uneasy**, like the floor is tilting and she needs to keep her balance.
Not **frightened**, because nearby practices are always short of doctors.
S1.quote: I'm salaried, not a partner, so I'm the kind of doctor whose sessions get trimmed first.
fieldNote: She sees her **contract type**, salaried rather than partner, as her real weak point.
Her plan leans on **hands-on skills** as the part a screen can't do.
Her **steady streak** shows: she will train once trusted colleagues say it's worth it.
She expects a **lost session** is realistic, which is real money even if she sounds composed.

steps.text: Sign up for the health board's AI results training in spring
Take the minor surgery and joint injection diploma for about 1,500
Push the flat purchase with Tomas back six months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before I'd even have the deposit saved. That's a lot to take in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say patients will still want a person in the room, which I do believe. I'd say it calmly, because people would be scared and they'd look to their doctor. I wouldn't post anything; there'd be enough panic online without me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, most of my day is thinking work: listening, working out what's serious, deciding on tests, writing it up. If a machine does that as well as me by 2028, the bit of me that's left is the physical exam and the hand on the shoulder, maybe a quarter of my day. The robots come three years later, so I'd have till about 2031 doing the hands-on bits, and after that I really don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd start the minor surgery diploma, not next year, now. I'd ask the senior partner to let me run the joint injection and coil-fitting clinics, because those need hands. And Tomas and I would stop saving for a flat and build the cash up to six months of costs. Taking on a mortgage on a doctor's job that might be gone by 2031 would be mad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly. Not panicked, because every doctor would be in the same boat and the government couldn't just let the health system fall over. But I'd lie awake doing sums, and my stomach would drop every time I opened the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would ask if all those years of medical school were wasted, because she paid for half my textbooks. I'd tell her no, that a doctor still has to be the one who answers for it when something goes wrong. I'm not sure I'd fully believe it while I was saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said patients will want a person, but also that most of your day could go. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I think. Patients will want a person, but the practice won't pay eight doctors for the part only a person can do. So I'd be one of fewer doctors, or doing fewer sessions, and I'd hope my injections and stitching keep me in the smaller group.

say: Patients will still want a **person in the room**, and I'd say it calmly.
I'd **stay off social media**, since there'd be enough panic there already.
think: About **three-quarters** of my day is thinking work a machine could do by 2028.
The **hands-on parts** might carry me to about 2031, and after that I don't know.
The practice won't pay **eight doctors** for the part only a person can do.

Ask to run the practice's **injection and coil clinics**, because they need hands.
Stop saving for a flat and build cash to **six months** of costs.
feel: **Alarmed**, lying awake doing sums, though not panicked.
Some comfort that **every doctor** would be in the same boat.
S2.quote: Taking on a mortgage on a doctor's job that might be gone by 2031 would be mad.
fieldNote: She separates **patient demand** for a human from what the practice will pay for.
Her **mum's question** about wasted medical school clearly stings her.
Two years kills the **flat plan** outright; she keeps cash rather than borrow.

steps.text: Start the minor surgery diploma this term instead of next year
Ask to run the practice's joint injection and coil clinics
Build savings up to six months of costs in the bank
Drop the plan to buy a flat with Tomas

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's better. I'd be thirty-two by then, which is enough time to actually do something rather than just react.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, that a doctor in the room still matters, but I'd add that we've got time and should use it. At work I'd push the practice to plan it out, which sessions change and when, instead of everyone pretending it isn't coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years means I can still buy the flat and be okay, if I'm careful. But I'd be watching the hiring: if Linden Road stops replacing doctors who leave around 2029, that's my sign. The hands-on part of my day would last till about 2034, so that's eight years in all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year, the diploma, same as before. Next year I'd add a women's health certificate, coils and contraceptive implants, because that's hands and conversation together. We'd still buy a flat, but a one-bed instead of two, so the mortgage could be paid on my partner Tomas's wage alone if my sessions drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, but it's a working kind of anxious. I'd have a list and a timeline, and that helps me sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you watch for, to know it's really coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two things. Whether the health board starts letting AI sign off routine results without a doctor, and whether practices stop advertising for salaried doctors. The moment I see both, I'd stop pretending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else in your life would this hit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, the practice nurse, would probably be fine for longer than me, because she does dressings and jabs all day. Tomas too, until robots can rewire a house. After all those exams, I might end up the shakiest earner in our home, and that's a strange thought.

say: A doctor in the room still matters, but **we have time** and should use it.
I'd push the practice to **plan which sessions** change and when.
think: Five years means I can still **buy the flat**, if I'm careful.
If the practice **stops replacing doctors** around 2029, that's my sign.
do: Finish the **minor surgery diploma** this year.
Add a **women's health certificate** for coils and implants next year.
Buy a **one-bed flat** instead of a two-bed, payable on Tomas's wage alone.
feel: **Anxious**, but a working kind of anxious with a list and a timeline.
S3.quote: We'd still buy a flat, but a one-bed instead of two, so the mortgage could be paid on my partner Tomas's wage alone if my sessions drop.
fieldNote: Five years turns her **alarm into a plan**, with warning signs to watch for.
She sizes the **mortgage to Tomas's wage**, quietly admitting her income is the riskier one.
She sees **nurses and electricians** outlasting her because their work is hands-on.

steps.text: Finish the minor surgery diploma at the teaching hospital this year
Take a women's health certificate in coils and implants next year
Buy a one-bed flat that Tomas's wage alone can cover

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a whole stage of life away, and the robots another three on top.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this one is manageable if the health system starts planning now. I'd probably say it most to the trainee doctors at the practice, because they're the ones who'd be mid-career when it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years lets me build a career that doesn't depend on being the one who thinks of the diagnosis. Maybe I become the doctor who checks what the AI decided and answers for it, or I move into procedures. And the honest bit: I'd probably have kids by then, and that's what would worry me, not 2036 itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, nothing dramatic. I'd do the diploma at a normal pace, start using the AI tools every day once they're standard at Linden Road, and Tomas and I would buy the two-bed flat as planned. I'd also put a bit extra into my pension, so that if work thins out in my forties, I'm not starting from zero.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in the background. It feels like knowing the boiler is old. You don't panic, you just start putting money aside for the new one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned kids. How does this change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still have them, probably around thirty. But I'd want my kids to grow up learning to do things with their hands as well as their heads, which is funny coming from a doctor. Six years of medical school, and I'd tell them to learn plumbing too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change your plan in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw AI doing a whole consultation on its own and patients liking it better, I'd move faster. Until then I'd take it a year at a time, like I take everything.

I'd tell the **trainee doctors**, since they'll be mid-career when it lands.
think: Ten years lets me become the doctor who **checks the AI** and answers for it.
My real worry is **having kids** by then, not the date itself.
do: Finish the **diploma** at a normal pace and use AI tools once they're standard.
Buy the **two-bed flat** with Tomas as planned.
Pay **extra into her pension** in case work thins out in her forties.
feel: **Uneasy** in the background, like knowing the boiler is old.
S4.quote: I'd want my kids to grow up learning to do things with their hands as well as their heads, which is funny coming from a doctor.
fieldNote: With ten years, her worry shifts from her job to her **future children**.
She pictures a role **checking AI decisions** and carrying the responsibility.
Her rhythm is **a year** at a time; only proof would make her move faster.

steps.text: Buy the two-bed flat with Tomas as planned
Use the practice's AI tools daily once they become standard
Pay extra into her pension each month from next year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years isn't enough to retrain or to save, and we'd lose the flat plan completely. What would help is the health board paying for doctors to train in hands-on skills, properly and quickly, and salaried doctors getting the same notice as partners when sessions are cut.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what patients think. My diabetic patient with the neat little notebook wouldn't want a screen reading his sugars back to him. I still think people like him will want a doctor who knows their name.

headlineQuote: After all those exams, I might end up the shakiest earner in our home, and that's a strange thought.
portrait: Olga is a **27-year-old salaried GP** at a busy suburban practice, renting above a bakery with Tomas, an electrician.
She is **steady with change**, adopting tools only once colleagues she trusts vouch for them.
She sees her **salaried contract**, not her skill, as her weak point when work is cut.
Across the scenarios her answer is **hands-on training** in minor surgery and women's health.
The **flat purchase** is her gauge: kept, shrunk or dropped depending on the timeline.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short to retrain or save.
whatWouldHelp: The health board **paying for fast training** in hands-on skills.
**Equal notice** for salaried doctors and partners when sessions are cut.
